title: Literary Devices and Close Reading
tagline: Imagery, symbolism, irony and tone, read closely enough to be written about precisely.

overview.intro: Literary devices are the difference between describing what a text says and explaining how it works. Because the prescribed drama, prose and poetry titles for this examination year are still pending verification against the official ISC list, this chapter trains the transferable skill the Paper 2 questions rest on: naming a device accurately, quoting the line that carries it, and saying what the device does to meaning, tone or feeling. Each family — figurative language, imagery and pattern, irony and tone, and structural choice — is taken through its members with original illustrative examples, so that when the set texts are confirmed the analytical method is already in hand. Close reading, the chapter’s working discipline, is the four-move sequence: notice, name, quote, explain.

facts.label: Four moves
facts.value: Notice the effect, name the device, quote the evidence, explain the work.

facts.label: Device families
facts.value: Figurative language; imagery and pattern; irony and tone; structure.

facts.label: Quotes earn
facts.value: A named device without a quotation is half an answer; a quotation without a name is the other half.

facts.label: Exam weight
facts.value: Paper 2 rewards precise terminology paired with close textual evidence.

learningOutcomes: Identify and distinguish the major figures of speech, including the common confusions.
Analyse how imagery, sound and pattern build a text’s effects.
Distinguish the three ironies and describe tone through evidence.
Explain how structure, viewpoint and narrative distance shape meaning.
Apply the notice–name–quote–explain sequence to a passage in short analytical answers.

learn.title: Figurative language: comparison and its relatives

blocks.text: Figurative language says one thing to mean another, and precision about which figure is at work separates a strong answer from a loose one. Simile compares using like or as: a face like stone promises hardness and stillness. Metaphor asserts the identity outright: the face is stone, which is stronger, because it offers no distance for the reader to stand in. Personification grants human action to the non-human — the wind worried the door — and its close relative pathetic fallacy lets weather or landscape carry the characters’ feelings. Hyperbole exaggerates to disclose urgency or absurdity, while its opposite litotes understates through a negated contrary: not bad meaning good. Metonymy substitutes the associated thing for the thing itself: the crown for the monarchy, the bench for the judiciary. Each figure makes a distinct promise to the reader, so an answer that names the figure must also say what the substitution adds that the literal statement would not have carried.

items: Simile keeps distance with like or as; metaphor closes it by asserting identity.
Personification gives human action to the non-human; pathetic fallacy ties it to weather or scene.
Hyperbole exaggerates to disclose urgency; litotes understates through negation.
Metonymy substitutes the associated entity: the crown for the monarchy.
Oxymoron holds contradictions together — bittersweet, deafening silence — to hold a tension.
Always follow the name with what the figure adds over the literal version.

items.text: “The fog came pouring in at every keyhole.”
items.note: Personification gives the fog a human verb, making the closing space feel deliberate rather than meteorological.

items.text: “He was not unaware of the danger.”
items.note: Litotes: the negated contrary understates, letting the danger stand as known without alarm being declared.

blocks.text: Imagery is language that addresses the senses, and analysis begins by naming which sense is being worked: visual, auditory, tactile, olfactory or gustatory, with kinesthetic covering movement. A passage that runs several senses at once creates immediacy; one that restricts itself to sight keeps the reader at the distance of an observer. Sound devices belong to the same craft: alliteration and assonance tune a line’s music, while onomatopoeia makes the sound enact its meaning — hissed, clattered. Beyond single words, pattern devices organise whole passages. Repetition drills an emphasis by returning to it, anaphora opens successive clauses with the same words to build pressure, and parallelism sets clauses of matching shape so that ideas appear of matching weight. A list, however, is not analysis: the examinable move is to connect the pattern to its purpose — what the repetition insists on, what the parallelism equates, what the sound makes the reader feel before the sense arrives.

items: Name the sense: visual, auditory, tactile, olfactory, gustatory, kinesthetic.
Several senses together create immediacy; sight alone keeps observational distance.
Alliteration and assonance tune sound; onomatopoeia enacts it.
Repetition insists; anaphora builds pressure at clause openings; parallelism equates weight.
Rhyme and rhythm in verse can signal resolution — or, when broken, signal disturbance.
Connect every pattern to its purpose; naming without purpose scores half.

items.text: “The rooms were quiet as a held breath.”
items.note: Auditory image plus simile: the silence is measured against a body, so stillness reads as suspense.

items.text: “We shall fight on the beaches, we shall fight on the landing grounds, we shall fight …”
items.note: Anaphora opens each clause identically, so the accumulation pressures the reader rather than merely informing.

items.meaning: Language addressing the senses, named by which sense it works.
Repetition of the same words at the openings of successive clauses.
Clauses of matching grammatical shape, implying ideas of matching weight.
A word whose sound enacts its meaning, such as hissed or clattered.

learn.title: Irony, tone and the speaker behind the words

blocks.text: Irony is the gap between what is said, what is meant and what is true, and it comes in three distinguishable kinds. Verbal irony says the opposite of the meaning — “What lovely weather” into a storm — and is the family that sarcasm belongs to, sarcasm being its hostile member. Situational irony occurs when the outcome reverses the expectation set up: the fire station burns down. Dramatic irony is created for an audience that knows more than a character: Juliet appears dead to the mourners and alive to the viewers, and every line she speaks lands twice. Tone is the attitude the words disclose towards their subject, and it must be inferred from diction and figure rather than asserted: dry, wry, bitter, deferential, amused, elegiac. The reliable method is lexical: pick the two words that carry the attitude, quote them, and name the tone they jointly produce. An answer that labels the tone without quoting the diction that produces it is an opinion; with the quotation it becomes an analysis.

items: Verbal irony says the opposite; situational reverses expectation; dramatic runs on unequal knowledge.
Sarcasm is hostile verbal irony, not a fourth kind.
Tone is inferred from diction and figure, never asserted from the plot.
Quote the two words that carry the attitude, then name the tone they produce.
Dramatic irony makes a character’s line land twice: what they mean and what the audience knows.
Free indirect style blurs narrator and character, often producing irony without quotation marks.

items.text: “The safety committee met, and unanimously recommended nothing.”
items.note: Situational irony: the body constituted for action resolves into inaction, and the flat adverb sharpens the joke.

items.text: “She said she was perfectly content, staring at the packed cases.”
items.note: Verbal claim contradicted by image — the tone is strained, and the evidence is the mismatch.

learn.title: Structure, viewpoint and the four moves of close reading

blocks.text: Structure is the writer’s management of time, viewpoint and emphasis, and it is the device family most visible to a question that asks how a text is organised. Begin with the shape: does the narrative run in order, loop back in flashback, or open in medias res and fill the gap later? Viewpoint decides what the reader can know: first person limits knowledge to the narrating self and colours everything with that self’s bias, while third-person limited stays with one consciousness and may still withhold. Narrative distance — how far the narration stands from the character’s idiom — controls whether the prose absorbs the character’s voice or frames it. Against this analysis stands the working method of the whole chapter: the four moves of close reading. Notice the effect in the reader; name the device with an exact term; quote the shortest line that carries it; explain what the device does to meaning, tone or feeling. Four moves, one paragraph, in that order — the sequence turns a reaction into an answer the mark scheme can reward.

items: Shape first: linear, flashback or in medias res — then what the shape withholds or delays.
Viewpoint limits knowledge and biases it; name whose consciousness controls the page.
Narrative distance decides whether prose absorbs a voice or frames it.
Free indirect style merges narrator and character, often carrying irony silently.
Close reading is four moves: notice, name, quote, explain — in that order.
One device per paragraph done fully beats three devices named without explanation.

items.text: Opening in medias res: a story begins at the trial and returns to the crime.
items.note: The structure withholds the crime, so suspense runs on how rather than whether, and the return reframes the opening judgement.

items.text: “It was a bright cold day in April, and the clocks were striking thirteen.”
items.note: A neutral third person registers one impossible detail, and the flat tone makes the strangeness factual rather than exclamatory.

items.meaning: Beginning in the middle of the action, with earlier events filled later.
The consciousness through which events and details are filtered.
How far the narration stands from the character’s idiom and thought.
Third-person narration coloured by a character’s voice without quotation.

figures.caption: Figure: The four moves of close reading in sequence
figures.description: Four connected panels in order: notice the reader’s effect, name the exact device, quote the shortest carrying line, explain the work on meaning, tone or feeling.
labels: order is fixed: reaction becomes analysis

figures.description: Three Venn-style diagrams: words against meaning for verbal irony, expectation against outcome for situational, and audience knowledge against character knowledge for dramatic.

keyPoints: Name the device exactly; simile, metaphor and personification are distinct answers.
Every name must be followed by what the device adds over the literal statement.
Imagery is named by sense; several senses together create immediacy.
Repetition insists, anaphora pressures, parallelism equates weight.
Three ironies: verbal (words vs meaning), situational (expectation vs outcome), dramatic (unequal knowledge).
Tone is inferred from diction — quote the words that carry the attitude.
Structure governs time, viewpoint and distance; each choice limits what the reader knows.
Close reading runs four moves: notice, name, quote, explain.
One device fully explained beats three devices merely named.
Dramatic irony makes a character’s line land twice: their meaning and the audience’s knowledge.
examFocus: Device questions need name plus quotation plus effect; two of the three is half an answer.
Do not confuse sarcasm with irony’s kinds — it is a tone inside verbal irony.
For tone, quote the diction before naming the tone; the label alone reads as opinion.
Structure questions ask what the arrangement withholds, delays or reframes.

vocabulary.meaning: A comparison holding distance open with like or as.
An asserted identity between two things without stated comparison.
Weather or landscape carrying the feelings of the scene’s people.
Understatement through a negated contrary, as in not unaware.
Identical words opening successive clauses to build pressure.
Effect produced when the audience knows more than the character.
The attitude towards the subject that diction and figure disclose.
Third-person narration taking on a character’s voice unquoted.

questions.prompt: “The wind clawed at the shutters.” This line is primarily:
questions.explanation: The human verb clawed gives the wind animal agency; no comparison marker and no sound-word carries the line.

questions.prompt: A character’s trust in a letter the audience knows to be forged creates:
questions.explanation: The audience holds knowledge the character lacks, which is the defining gap of dramatic irony.

questions.prompt: “The crown has spoken.” The device here is:
questions.explanation: The associated object stands for the institution — metonymy compresses the association rather than symbolising across a text.

questions.prompt: Which analysis best fits the repetition of “never” in “Never in the field of human conflict was so much owed by so many to so few”?
options: It places a negation first to make the uniqueness of the debt the sentence’s opening claim
It creates suspense for the clause that follows
questions.answer: It places a negation first to make the uniqueness of the debt the sentence’s opening claim
questions.explanation: Fronting the negative makes the unprecedented scale the first thing the ear receives, so the emphasis lands on uniqueness before the debt is counted.

questions.prompt: A comparison using the words like or as is called a __________ .
questions.explanation: The comparison marker keeps speaker and reader apart; the equivalent asserted identity is a metaphor.

questions.prompt: Language that makes a sound enact its meaning, such as hissed or clattered, is called __________ .
questions.explanation: The word performs the sound it names, adding auditory immediacy without an extra descriptive clause.

questions.prompt: Distinguish situational irony from dramatic irony with one original example of each.
questions.answer: Situational irony lives in the event: the outcome reverses what the setup led the reader to expect, as when the town’s brand-new fire station is the building lost to a stove fire — expectation and result contradict each other. Dramatic irony lives in unequal knowledge: the audience knows something a character does not, as when a audience watches a character hide a letter in a stage drawing that everyone can see will be opened. The first is a reversal of expectation; the second is a gap of awareness, and it typically makes each of the unaware character’s lines land twice.
questions.explanation: The kinds are told apart by where the gap lies: words against meaning, expectation against outcome, audience against character.

questions.prompt: Explain what the pathetic fallacy adds that plain weather description does not, with an example.
questions.answer: Plain weather description records conditions; pathetic fallacy charges them with the feelings of the people in the scene, so the surroundings become evidence of mood rather than fact. In “the rain kept time with her restlessness at the window”, the weather does not simply fall, it synchronises with her state, and the reader receives her agitation through the scene instead of through authorial statement. The device therefore deepens mood without direct comment, keeps the narration inside the world of the story, and lets a later change of weather register as a change in feeling without anyone saying so.
questions.explanation: Charging weather or scene with human feeling lets mood enter through the description instead of authorial comment.

questions.prompt: Apply the four moves of close reading to the line “She was a small house with a large grief.” Write one analytical paragraph.
questions.answer: Notice: the line unsettles before it explains — a person arrives as a building, and the building carries sorrow. Name: the governing device is metaphor, asserting identity between woman and house, supported by transferred epithet logic in large grief, since grief belongs to the person while size belongs to the house. Quote: “a small house with a large grief” is the shortest span carrying the effect, the contrast of small and large doing the emphasis inside it. Explain: the metaphor collapses the distance between observer and subject, so the reader does not compare her to a house but sees her as one, making her shrinkage and her burden architectural — she is narrow, weathered, holding something too big for her frame; the opposition of the adjectives also implies that what defines her is not her size but the scale of what she carries, and the past-tense was sets the whole reading at a distance of loss, as a memory rather than a present sighting.
questions.explanation: Notice, name, quote, explain: each move supplies one element the analytical paragraph needs to earn full marks.

questions.prompt: A candidate writes: “The author uses lots of imagery and it makes the reader feel sad. This shows the theme.” Evaluate this answer and rewrite it to full analytical strength.
questions.answer: The answer fails on all four moves of close reading at once. It never names a device precisely — lots of imagery is a quantity, not a device — it quotes nothing, it identifies no effect beyond a generic feels sad, and this shows the theme asserts a link without demonstrating it, so the examiner can award almost nothing against a rubric requiring name, evidence and explained work. The rewrite: the passage builds elegiac tone through a restricted auditory image — the line quotes “nothing louder than the gate’s complaint” — whose personification of the gate gives the only complaint in a silent scene to an object rather than a person. Naming personification and quoting the span fixes the first two moves; explaining that the silence transfers the residents’ unspoken grief onto the hardware of the house, so the setting grieves in their place, fixes the third; and the thematic claim then follows demonstrated rather than declared — the scene argues that in this place sorrow has become environment, and the reader receives it as atmosphere before receiving it as event.
questions.explanation: A precise device name, a quoted span and the demonstrated work on meaning are what the rubric rewards over generic praise.
